title: When the Verdict Burns
premise: August Galloway, a true-crime podcaster who moved to the fading town of Marrow Bend to document its coldest case—the 1994 disappearance of heiress Delphine Voss—receives a confession letter postmarked the day after the funeral of Delphine's mother, claiming Delphine was killed by someone still living there. As August investigates, they discover the letter's author is dying and being picked off the suspect list one by one, while the town's founding families close ranks to protect the inheritance that Delphine's death secured. August realizes the confession was sent to them deliberately: the dying writer, Delphine's secret half-sibling, wanted an outsider to finish what justice couldn't. In the end, August exposes the killer—Delphine's own brother, now the town's beloved patriarch—at a live recording of the podcast's final episode, choosing belonging to the truth over belonging to Marrow Bend.
about_author: Oscar Halloran is a former court reporter who spent a decade transcribing small-town trials before turning to fiction. He writes mysteries about the secrets communities keep to stay standing.

chapters.title: Alphabetized Ghosts
chapters.summary: August Galloway's POV. August catalogs the Voss case files in their cluttered studio, establishing three years of careful distance from Marrow Bend's grief. The town attends Edith Voss's funeral; August records it from the back pew. Emotional beat: controlled detachment that hints at loneliness beneath the method.

chapters.title: Postmarked the Day After
chapters.summary: August's POV. A confession letter arrives claiming Delphine Voss was murdered in 1994, signed only 'the one who watched.' August verifies the postmark—dated the day after Edith's funeral. Emotional beat: the thrill of a lifetime's story colliding with dread that someone wanted them specifically to receive it.

chapters.title: The Families Who Built the Bend
chapters.summary: August's POV. August profiles the Voss, Crane, and Ashford dynasties whose fortunes intertwined with the town's founding. Research reveals Delphine's inheritance would have split the estate among all three families—unless she died before turning twenty-five. Emotional beat: the dawning shape of motive, cold and financial.

chapters.title: Episode Forty-One
chapters.summary: August's POV, interwoven with podcast audio transcripts. August releases a cautious episode reopening the case, and within hours receives threats, flowers, and a burned cassette tape left on their porch. Emotional beat: the town's mask of hospitality slipping to show teeth.

chapters.title: What the River Kept
chapters.summary: August's POV. At the drowned quarry where Delphine's car was found, August meets Ruth Crane, now elderly, who lets slip that Delphine had a secret—'a sister nobody was meant to know.' Emotional beat: the first crack in thirty years of silence.

chapters.title: The Half-Brother's Ledger
chapters.summary: August's POV. Digging through probate records, August uncovers evidence of an illegitimate Voss child born in 1968, erased from the family Bible. The confession letter's handwriting matches samples from this man, Elias Voss. Emotional beat: identification of the letter-writer, and the question of why he confessed now.

chapters.title: A Dying Man's Address
chapters.summary: August's POV. August tracks Elias to a hospice two counties away. He confirms he watched the murder happen as a teenager—but swears he didn't do it, and that the killer's name is written somewhere 'the family would never look.' Emotional beat: fragile alliance formed between the invisible podcaster and the erased brother.

chapters.title: Thirty-Year Alibis
chapters.summary: August's POV, with flashbacks to 1994 from Elias's letters. August cross-examines the alibis of that June night: patriarch Marcus Voss claims he was at a lodge meeting; brother Theodore was 'asleep'; Ruth Crane was at the hospital. Each alibi is airtight—and each was corroborated by the same two witnesses. Emotional beat: the sick elegance of coordinated lies.

chapters.title: The Lodge on Ashford Hill
chapters.summary: August's POV. August infiltrates a gathering of the town's old families, posing as a genealogy researcher. They overhear Theodore Voss—now the town's patriarch—steering the conversation away from Delphine with practiced charm. Emotional beat: proximity to power, and the vertigo of being noticed by it.

chapters.title: Someone Starts Burning Files
chapters.summary: August's POV. The county archive room catches fire; August's own storage unit is ransacked, and their interview recordings with Elias are stolen. Only the physical letters remain, hidden in August's mattress. Emotional beat: the investigation has stopped being a story and become a target.

chapters.title: Ruth Breaks
chapters.summary: August's POV. Ruth Crane, confronted with the burned cassette, admits she saw Marcus Voss's truck at the quarry that night—and that the lodge meeting was a fabrication the families rehearsed together. Emotional beat: grief and guilt finally cracking a lifetime of complicity.

chapters.title: Where the Family Would Never Look
chapters.summary: August's POV. Following Elias's riddle, August searches the Voss family plot and finds Delphine's headstone is a false marker—beneath the memorial slab, a sealed tin box holds her real diary. Emotional beat: the dead speaking at last, and the weight of what she recorded.

chapters.title: Delphine's Voice
chapters.summary: Delphine's diary entries, 1993–1994, presented as found text. She documents discovering her father's embezzlement, her plan to dissolve the inheritance and give it to the town, and her fear of Theodore, who 'smiles like he's already won.' Emotional beat: a bright, doomed intelligence reaching across thirty years.

chapters.title: The Inheritance That Ate a Town
chapters.summary: August's POV. August maps how Delphine's death preserved the estate, funded the families' fortunes, and bought the silence of half of Marrow Bend—including the sheriff who closed the case. Emotional beat: horror at how thoroughly corruption was laundered into civic virtue.

chapters.title: Threats in the Shape of Kindness
chapters.summary: August's POV. Theodore Voss invites August to dinner, offering sponsorship of the podcast and gently revealing he knows where August's estranged sister lives. Emotional beat: the seduction and menace of power—August understands they can be bought or broken, and that refusing means war.

chapters.title: Elias Slips Away
chapters.summary: August's POV. Rushing to the hospice, August finds Elias unconscious after a 'reaction' to medication—and a visitor's log showing Theodore's lawyer was there an hour before. Elias wakes just long enough to whisper that the confession was a message: 'Finish it, because I couldn't.' Emotional beat: the ally's clock running out.

chapters.title: The Sheriff's Old Report
chapters.summary: August's POV. August obtains the original 1994 police file from the retired deputy who kept a copy out of conscience. It shows evidence of struggle at the quarry, suppressed; tire impressions matching Theodore's truck, dismissed. Emotional beat: cold, hard corroboration—and the terror of holding it.

chapters.title: One by One
chapters.summary: August's POV. Ruth Crane is hospitalized after a fall down her stairs; the retired deputy leaves town abruptly. August realizes the loose ends are being tied off and that they are the last one. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into resolve—running is no longer possible.

chapters.title: The Last Episode
chapters.summary: August's POV. August announces a live finale at the Marrow Bend grange hall, promising to close the Voss case forever. Theodore attends in the front row, confident and magnanimous. August lays out the diary, the suppressed report, and the alibi conspiracy before a packed room. Emotional beat: the trap closing in both directions.

chapters.title: When the Verdict Burns
chapters.summary: August's POV. Theodore's composure fractures on record as August plays Ruth's statement and reveals Elias's dying testimony; the sheriff's son, now a state trooper, arrests him as the crowd watches. Theodore's parting words: 'She was going to burn it all down. I just burned her first.' Emotional beat: catharsis, justice, and the cost of hearing it said aloud.

chapters.title: What Belonging Costs
chapters.summary: August's POV. In the aftermath, the town splits between gratitude and resentment; some doors that were closed to August for three years open, while others close forever. Elias dies peacefully, his name added to the family Bible at last. Emotional beat: mourning the version of belonging August can never have here.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair at the Mic
chapters.summary: August's POV. August records the true final episode—not about the Vosses, but about the town itself, the people who stayed silent and the ones who couldn't. They pack the studio, leave the key with Ruth's nurse, and drive out at dawn. Emotional beat: bittersweet departure; August belonged to the truth all along.
